Question 1¶

EDA on Missing data

  • The only columns that had missing data in the original MNF set were the EliteQBs column and the two SuperBowl Odds columns. Both of them had missing values across seasons and the poorgames/viewership target columns were pretty much the same (10% or so for poor game rate) with or without values in those so that would suggest missing at random. Due to that, I used median imputation for these as dropping the affected rows would make us lose nearly 30% of our dataset.

Feature Engineering

  • I decided to use a few things that I knew about football to make some features. One of the things was that cable vs over air affects viewership. Another was that there are teams that have significantly more fans than others, so I made an indicator for that. The indicator ranges from 0 to 2 with 0 being no popular teams and 2 being 2 popular teams. I also wanted to quantify the perception of how good of a game it was. Ideally, I'd have a % of games won going into the matchup type of column as two undefeated teams brings a lot of excitement, but I used a total superbowl odds sum and a total points sum to try and capture that.

a)¶

  • RMSE for the models is as follows:
    • Lasso: 0.8771776038715349
    • KNN: 0.8898934700555123
    • Random Forest: 0.8721127256752681
    • Gradient Boosting: 0.8789392129105993
    • Neural Net: 0.8765689579300716
  • Given that Lasso Regression is more explainable with coefficients, I decided to go with that one even though the Random Forest model is the best RMSE and the Neural Net is slightly better than Lasso.

b)¶

  • I scored the Lasso with the best parameters on to the 2019 data after running it through my clean data and feature engineering pipeline. Saved the dataframe with predictions for the next step. The coefficients that were most important were:
    • popular_teams 0.233
    • log_WorstOddsSB -0.166
    • BestFranchiseRank -0.148
    • MaxScoreAvg 0.147

Question 2¶

a)¶

  • ROC AUC for the models is as follows:
    • Lasso Logistic: 0.7187153931339978
    • KNN: 0.6590143964562569
    • Random Forest: 0.6850276854928017
    • Gradient Boosting: 0.7182059800664452
    • Neural Net: 0.7155177187153932
    • SVM: 0.66952934662237
  • Still not a stellar model, but that is probably a given, given our feature limitations. Due to Lasso Logistic being the highest ROC AUC and the simplest, I am choosing that.

b)¶

  • I scored the Lasso Logistic with the best paramaters on to the 2019 feature engineered data. Saved the dataframe with predictions for Question 3. The coefficients that were most important were:
    • popular_teams -0.650
    • SuperBowlChamp -0.475
    • Week 0.323
    • log_odds_sum 0.316

Question 3¶

  • exported to excel

Question 4¶

  • They disagree most for Bears @ Washington and Cowboys @ Giants with 6 and 5 differences in rank respectively. Otherwise the gaps are at most 3 between ranking, so they're close. The spearman coefficient for these (a thing I learned about at work when I was comparing a sales ranking model, funny enough) at -0.83 is good given that Spearman ranges from 1 to -1 where 0 would mean no agreement and then closer to either 1 or -1 means agreement and just shows for which direction they agree so it's showing negative correlation which is what we expect given that it's looking at viewership (where higher = better) and poorgame (where lower is better). While they both show that popular_teams is most important, the regresser keys more on the odds, franchise rank, and scoer average where the classifier goes more on the superbowl champ, week, and the log odds sum.

Question 5¶

  • Work and some of the thought to get there is shown at the bottom of this notebook. However, to summarize what I arrived at there, the probability of it being a poor game has to be above 1/3 given that it's 400k cost to reserve / 1.2 million cost if you don't. The Lasso model I landed on doesn't predict any of the games to hit that probability threshold of greater than ~0.33333 of being a bad game. The caveat is that we didn't perfectly calibrate this model and that is something I usually look at more when doing probabilities (but I decided against that for this given that it's not in the scope of what we covered in class). If this was the real world, I'd potentially suggest incurring that 400k cost for the Broncos @ Raiders especially considering that the two different classifier and regression models do uniformly rank that as the worst game and the predicted probability is nearing the 1/3 at 0.309377. The other thing to note too is that the prevailing rate the model learned from for poor games (about 10%) predicts that 1.7 games (or 2 if you round) will be poor and that has been consistent throughout the seasons. Given that, it almost changes the scope of the question to say "I know there will be at least one bad game, find me the one with the highest odds of being bad and let's spend the extra money on that". If that was more the business direciton, I would recommend going for Broncos @ Raiders.

Clean Data¶

In [29]:
# transform PoorGame and Election Year to binary
# make date a datetime object
# clean column names to remove spaces

YES_NO = {"Yes": 1, "No": 0}

def clean(df):
    df = df.copy()
    df.columns = df.columns.str.replace(" ", "", regex=False)

    df["ElectionYear"] = pd.to_numeric(df["ElectionYear"].replace(YES_NO)).astype("int64")
    df["PoorGame"] = pd.to_numeric(df["PoorGame"].replace(YES_NO)).astype("Int64")

    df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], format="%m/%d/%Y")
    return df

mndfclean = clean(mndf)

Feature Engineering¶

In [40]:
# I want to make a feature that captures whether the game was on cable or over air
# I want to log scale the odds columns since they are skewed, and then I also want to add those together to see how good the teams are
# I want to add together the max score average and min score average to get a total score average to see how 'explosive' the offenses are
# as an aside I wish they had % of games won going into the game and also a % of games won over the past couple of seasons as that could help determine late season matchup quality better
# I also want to make a popular teams since I know Green Bay, Chicago, Cowboys, New England, Pittsburgh, Giants, Jets, Eagles, and Niners all have large fan bases
### I want to make this popular teams feature be 0 if no popular teams are playing, 1 if one of the teams is popular, and 2 if both teams are popular

popular_teams = {
    "Dallas Cowboys", "Green Bay Packers", "Pittsburgh Steelers", "Chicago Bears",
    "New York Giants", "New York Jets", "Philadelphia Eagles", "San Francisco 49ers", "New England Patriots",
}

def feature_engineering(df):
    df = df.copy()
    df["cable"] = (df["Network"] == "ESPN").astype(int)
    df["popular_teams"] = (df["AwayTeam"].isin(popular_teams).astype(int)
                           + df["HomeTeam"].isin(popular_teams).astype(int))

    for col in ["WorstOddsSB", "BestOddsSB"]:
        df[f"log_{col}"] = np.log(df[col])
    df["log_odds_sum"] = df["log_WorstOddsSB"] + df["log_BestOddsSB"]
    df["total_score_avg"] = df["MaxScoreAvg"] + df["MinScoreAvg"]
    return df.drop(columns=["WorstOddsSB", "BestOddsSB"])

Question 5¶

In [72]:
# ok so we have the cost to reserve which is 400k, we have the cost of a miss which is 1.2m
# we only want to reserve when p x 1200k > 400k which is p > 1/3

reserve_cost = 400000

cost_of_miss = 1200000

threshold = reserve_cost / cost_of_miss

# get dataset
profit_question = games_19_clean[["Game", "AwayTeam", "HomeTeam", "Week"]].copy()

# predict the poorgame probability
profit_question["poorgame_prob"]  = predict_poorgame

# add in the cost of reserving column
profit_question["expected_reserve_cost"] = reserve_cost

# add in the cost of missing column multiplied by the poorgame prediction
profit_question["expected_no_reserve_cost"] = predict_poorgame * cost_of_miss

# classify them based on if p > 1/3 which is our threshold
profit_question["classify_worth_reserving"] = profit_question["poorgame_prob"] > threshold

display(profit_question.sort_values("poorgame_prob", ascending=False))
